subtype: Approach: working backward from the audience's need [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday, 11 p.m.
Final-year project review on Friday. Twelve minutes in front of three professors who decide whether our water-filter project gets lab funding for next semester.
My first draft had 31 slides. Every experiment, every failed prototype, every graph. I was proud of it. Then Ujjwal asked, 'What does the panel actually have to decide?' I stopped. They don't need to know everything we did. They need to decide one thing: is this worth another semester?
So I asked myself: what would convince me, if I were them? That it works, that it's cheap, and what the next step needs. That's it.
I cut it to 11 slides. The six failed prototypes became one slide called 'what we learned'. The opening line is now the answer: 'Our filter removes 90% of bacteria at a cost of 40 rupees, and we need one more semester to test it in villages.'
Scary to delete so much. But it feels right.
– Zeenat

qa.a: Zeenat felt scared to delete so much work that had been a source of pride, but settled that the shorter talk feels right.

qa.a: They get the answer in the first line and the facts they need to decide, which makes their job easier.

Seminar talk on Thursday: fifteen minutes on our campus waste survey. Sarika, my project partner, wanted to open the slide software straight away and start picking templates. I said no, paper first.
We took an A3 sheet and drew twelve boxes. In each box we wrote what the slide must do: problem, method, result, or next step. Box 1: 'Hostels throw away 40 kg of food daily', with a sketch of a bin. Box 5: a quick bar chart. Box 11: what we want the college to change.
Then we asked of each box: does this help the story? Three boxes were just nice photos of us sorting rubbish. Out. One was a table of every bin's weight; it became one sentence on another slide.
Nine boxes left. Tonight we made the actual slides in forty minutes, because every decision was already on the paper.

'Ready? Timer's on,' Reena said, holding up her phone. 'Ten minutes. Go.'
Hrithik stood in the hostel common room, facing her and a row of empty chairs. 'Good morning. Our project looked at why tomato prices swing so wildly in our district...'

Hrithik sat down on a chair. 'That's my second run today. The first one was long too. I just didn't time it.'

I'm Tanuja, and before my first big class presentation I thought rehearsal meant reading my slides in my head. My sister made me do it properly.
The first run, alone in my room, out loud, with the phone timer: fourteen minutes. The limit was ten. I had no idea where the time went.
The second run I timed each part. Introduction: one minute. Background: two. The middle part, where I explained my survey method, took seven minutes. Seven! I'd been explaining every single question in the questionnaire.
I cut the method to three questions as examples and one sentence about the rest. The third run I did for my classmate Imran in an empty classroom after lunch. Ten minutes and twenty seconds. He said the middle still dragged a little, so I cut one more example.
On the day, I finished at 9:50. I've never felt so calm at the front of a room.

qa.a: Seven minutes.

qa.a: Tanuja felt calm and in control, which had never happened before at the front of a room.

qa.q: What else could Tanuja add to the rehearsal next time?

Dear Lakshmi,
You asked how my big presentation went. Honestly? Badly, and I know why.
I was so scared of forgetting something that I wrote everything on the slides. Full paragraphs. Some slides had eight bullet points of two lines each. My plan was simple: if my mind went blank, I'd just read.
My mind didn't go blank. I read anyway, because it was there. About three slides in, I saw the professor had already finished the slide and was looking at her phone. Two students in the front row were whispering. They could read faster than I could talk, so there was nothing left for me to add.
The worst moment was the end, when she asked a question and I realised I'd been reading so hard I had barely thought about what I was saying.
Next time: fewer words, more pictures, and notes on a card only I can see.
Sabina

qa.a: Keep only a few words or a picture on each slide and put the full points on a card, so the audience listens instead of reading.

Mehak, before you make your slides, let me, Rafiq, confess the worst fifteen minutes of my college life.
The departmental seminar, third year. I was terrified of freezing, so I typed my whole speech onto the slides. Every word. White background, small black text, twenty slides.
I stood there and read. Slide one. Slide two. By slide four I could hear chairs creaking. People had already read ahead and were waiting for me to catch up. Someone at the back yawned so loudly the class laughed. I didn't look up once, because if I looked up I'd lose my place in the paragraph.
Afterwards my friend said, 'Why did you even come? We could've just read the file.' He was joking, but he was right.
So please: a few words on the slide, the rest in your head or on a card. They came to hear you.

Bhavna came to me at 6 p.m. yesterday, pale, saying she had never spoken in a hall that big. Instead of more practice, I asked her to sit, close her eyes and walk me through tomorrow.

Today I watched her climb the three steps, lower the mic, glance at the clock and say her first sentence clearly. She said afterwards the first minute felt 'like I'd already been there'. I'll try this with the others.

Irawati's project on monsoon crop yields is one of the strongest this year; I've seen her data. She told me before the session she hadn't rehearsed. 'I know it inside out,' she said.

At ten minutes I had to stop her. The main result, that one change in sowing raised yields by a fifth, never appeared on screen. The judges marked her down for an incomplete talk.

Three days before my thesis defence, I asked my friend Ramesh to be as mean as possible. I'm Farhan, and I'd heard the panel liked to grill people.
We sat in the empty seminar room. Ramesh took the professors' chair and fired five questions at me. Why this method and not another? What's the biggest weakness in your data? How would you explain this to a farmer? What if the rainfall pattern changes? What would you do with another year?
I answered out loud and wrote each answer in two or three lines on a card. Three came out fine. Two, the weakness and the rainfall question, came out as mumbling. I starred those and spent the next two evenings reading.
At the defence, the panel asked the weakness question almost word for word. I looked at the professor and gave my three lines, calmly. I nearly laughed. Ramesh had been meaner.

subtype: Approach: emotion-aware handling of nerves [Revision]

I'm Maria, and I knew my voice would shake. It always does in the first minute. So when I planned my presentation for the marketing competition, I planned for that too: a glass of water on the table, and a note at the top of my card that said 'slow down, it's normal'.
The first slide went fine. Then on the second, I heard my voice go thin and wobbly, and I saw Chetan, my teammate, glance at me.
Before, I would have rushed to get it over with. This time I stopped. Counted two in my head. Took a sip of water. Looked at the card: slow down, it's normal. Then I started the slide again, a little slower.
The shake didn't vanish, but it faded by slide four. By the end I was actually enjoying it. Chetan said later that from the audience, the pause looked like I was letting a point sink in.

qa.q: What did Maria's card say at the top?
qa.a: 'slow down, it's normal'.

qa.q: What did Maria feel on the second slide, and how did Maria respond?
qa.a: Maria felt nervous as the voice went thin and wobbly, but stayed calm enough to pause, sip water and slow down as planned.

qa.q: What else could Maria add to the plan for the next competition?
qa.a: A slow breath before the first slide, so the nerves are eased even earlier.

qa.q: How did the pause look to Chetan in the audience?
qa.a: To Chetan it looked deliberate, like letting a point sink in, not like nerves.

grounding: Shows a student who planned for a shaky voice pausing, sipping water and slowing down after the first slide, and finishing steadily.

subtype: Approach: emotion-aware handling of nerves [Revision]
passage:
Lecturer's note – Tarun, final-year presentations, Batch B
Manoj told me last week that he freezes in front of groups, so I suggested he plan for it: expect the shaky voice, keep water nearby, and slow down on purpose if it happens.
Today his voice cracked on his second slide. I saw his hand tremble on the clicker. He stopped, put the clicker down, took a sip from his bottle, and said, 'Let me say that again.' He repeated the sentence at half the speed.
From there it steadied. By the results section he was pointing at the graph and looking at the room. He finished in eleven minutes, with one question answered well.
Afterwards he said, 'I was shaking, but I knew it would happen, so it didn't scare me as much.' I've marked him on content, and noted a real improvement in delivery.

qa.a: 'Let me say that again.'

qa.a: He still felt nervous and shaky, but expecting it made the fear smaller and let him recover calmly.

Raghav hesitated. 'Honestly? I didn't know what you found until the second-last slide.'
Nidhi nodded. 'You spent ages on the method. When the result came, I'd stopped paying attention.'
Ayesha felt a flash of annoyance. She'd worked hard on that method section. For a second she wanted to defend it. Then she thought about what she'd want as a listener, and wrote in her notebook: 'Result buried. Move it up.'
Two weeks later, at the next department seminar, her second slide said, in big letters: 'Reading aloud to toddlers increased their word count by 30% in eight weeks.' The method came after, shorter. When she looked out, Raghav gave her a thumbs-up.

Subject: Thank you for the honest feedback
Dear Sarita,
Thank you for staying back after my presentation on Thursday to tell me what didn't work. I'll admit, when you said you only understood the point in the last minute, part of me felt stung. I'd spent a week on those slides.
But you were right, and so was Pranjal when I asked him the same thing. I looked at the talk again: the key finding, that the new bus timings cut waiting time by a third, was on slide 14 of 15. Everything before it was background and method.
So for the conference next month I've moved it to slide 2. The method now comes after, in four slides instead of nine. I've also added a closing slide that repeats the finding in one line.
Would you be willing to watch a practice run next Friday? I'd value your eyes on it again.
Jahnavi

qa.q: On which slide was the key finding?
qa.a: Slide 14 of 15.
